paragraphs.context: there lived a poor fisherman called Arsheesh, and with him there lived
paragraphs.mainIdea: Shasta lives with a poor fisherman called Arsheesh. Arsheesh is hard on him when the fish sell badly, and Shasta has a lot of work.
paragraphs.simple: In those days, far south in Calormen, a poor fisherman called Arsheesh lived by a small arm of the sea. A boy lived with him and called him Father. The boy's name was Shasta. On most days Arsheesh went out in his boat in the morning to fish. In the afternoon he put his donkey to a cart and loaded the cart with fish. Then he went about a mile south to the village to sell the fish. If they sold well, he came home in a fairly good mood and said nothing to Shasta. If they sold badly, he found fault with Shasta and maybe hit him. There was always something to find fault with, because Shasta had a lot of work to do. He mended and washed the nets, cooked the supper and cleaned the cottage where they both lived.

paragraphs.context: These were great days for Shasta, and every day better than the last
paragraphs.mainIdea: Shasta gets better at riding, and Bree is a patient teacher. Bree does not like to talk about the Tisroc's wars. He wants to fight in the Narnian wars as a free Horse.
paragraphs.simple: These were very good days for Shasta. Each day was better than the last, because he grew stronger and fell less often. Bree still said Shasta sat like a bag of flour in the saddle. He said he would be ashamed to be seen with Shasta on the main road, even if it was safe. But Bree was a patient teacher, though his words were rude. No one can teach riding as well as a horse. Shasta learned to trot, to canter and to jump. He learned to stay on when Bree stopped or turned to the left or right without warning. Bree said you might have to do that at any moment in a battle. Shasta asked to hear about the battles and wars in which Bree had carried the Tarkaan. Bree told of long forced marches, of crossing fast rivers, and of charges. He told of fierce fights between horsemen, where the war horses fought too. They were all stallions, trained to bite and kick, and to rear up at the right moment. Then the weight of the horse and of the rider came down on the enemy. But Bree did not want to talk about the wars as often as Shasta wanted to hear. He said they were only the Tisroc's wars, and he had fought in them as a slave and a dumb beast. He said he wanted the Narnian wars, where he would fight as a free Horse among his own people.

paragraphs.context: the best place would be the Tombs of the Ancient Kings
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bree says they should meet at the Tombs of the Ancient Kings if they get separated in Tashbaan. Then Hwin says the real problem is how to get through the city.
paragraphs.simple: Bree said the first thing to do was to choose a place on the far side of Tashbaan where they would all promise to meet. They would need it if they were separated while passing the city. He said the best place was the Tombs of the Ancient Kings, on the very edge of the desert. He said they were like great stone beehives and easy to see. He said the best part was that none of the Calormenes would go near them. They think ghouls haunt the place and they are afraid of it. Aravis asked if ghouls did not really haunt it. Bree said he was a free Narnian horse and did not believe these Calormene tales. Then Shasta said he was not a Calormene either, and did not care a straw about these old stories. That was not quite true. It rather impressed Aravis, but at the moment it also annoyed her. She said she did not mind any number of ghouls either. So they agreed that the Tombs would be their meeting place on the other side of Tashbaan. They felt they were getting on well, until Hwin humbly said that the real problem was not where to go after they got through Tashbaan. It was how to get through it.

paragraphs.context: The leader of the fair-haired men suddenly pointed at Shasta
paragraphs.mainIdea: The leader of the fair-haired men calls Shasta their runaway. He seizes him and smacks him.
paragraphs.simple: But there was no time to enjoy the sight, because at once a really dreadful thing happened. The leader of the fair-haired men suddenly pointed at Shasta and cried out that there was their runaway. He seized Shasta by the shoulder. Then he gave Shasta a smack. It was not a cruel one that makes you cry. It was a sharp one that lets you know you are in disgrace. Then he spoke, still shaking Shasta.

paragraphs.context: his first impulse was to say that he was only poor Arsheesh
paragraphs.mainIdea: Shasta cannot say who he is, because people would ask about his horse and Aravis. Bree and Aravis cannot help him.
paragraphs.simple: Shasta's first thought was to say that he was only poor Arsheesh the fisherman's son, and that the foreign lord was wrong. But in that crowded place he did not want to start explaining who he was or what he was doing. People would soon ask where he got his horse and who Aravis was. Then he would lose any chance of getting through Tashbaan. His next thought was to look at Bree for help. But Bree did not want the crowd to know that he could talk, and he looked as stupid as a horse can look. Shasta did not even dare to look at Aravis, for fear of drawing attention. There was no time to think, because the leader of the Narnians spoke at once.

paragraphs.context: He was in fact a Faun, which is a creature Shasta had never seen
paragraphs.mainIdea: Shasta sees that the speaker is a Faun, half man and half goat. His name is Tumnus.
paragraphs.simple: A voice spoke to the Kings and Queens. When Shasta turned to look, he nearly jumped out of his skin with surprise. The speaker was one of the queer people he had seen out of the corner of his eye when he came into the room. He was about as tall as Shasta. From the waist up he was like a man. His legs were hairy and shaped like a goat's, and he had a goat's hoofs and a tail. His skin was rather red, and he had curly hair, a short pointed beard and two little horns. He was a Faun, a creature Shasta had never seen a picture of or heard of. His name was Tumnus. Queen Susan's sister Lucy had met him on her very first day in Narnia. He was a good deal older now, because Peter, Susan, Edmund and Lucy had been Kings and Queens of Narnia for several years.
hardWords: out of the corner of his eye

paragraphs.context: It never came into his head to tell these Narnians the whole truth
paragraphs.mainIdea: Shasta does not dare tell the Narnians the truth. He thinks they would never let him leave the house alive, because he has heard their plans.
paragraphs.simple: Shasta never thought of telling the Narnians the whole truth and asking for help. Shasta had been brought up by a hard, closefisted man like Arsheesh. So Shasta was in the habit of never telling grown-ups anything if he could help it. He thought they would always spoil or stop what you were trying to do. He thought the Narnian King might be friendly to the two horses, because they were Talking Beasts of Narnia. But he thought the King would hate Aravis because she was a Calormene. The King would sell her for a slave or send her back to her father. Shasta thought he did not dare to say he was not Prince Corin. He had heard all their plans. If they knew he was not one of them, they would never let him out of the house alive. They would fear that he would tell the Tisroc, and they would kill him. If the real Corin came back, it would all come out. The writer says Shasta had no idea how noble and free-born people behave.

paragraphs.context: A boy in the street made a beastly joke about Queen Susan
paragraphs.mainIdea: Corin tells Shasta what happened to him in the street. He knocked down a boy and the boy's brother, and he got away from the Watch.
paragraphs.simple: Corin says a boy in the street made a bad joke about Queen Susan, so he knocked the boy down. The boy ran howling into a house, and his big brother came out. So Corin knocked the big brother down too. Then they all followed him until they met three old men with spears, called the Watch. He fought the Watch, and they knocked him down. It was getting dark by then. The Watch took him away to lock him up somewhere. He asked them if they would like a stoup of wine, and they said yes. He took them to a wine shop and got them some, and they sat down and drank until they fell asleep. Then he thought it was time to leave, and he came out quietly. He found the first boy, who had started all the trouble, still standing about. So he knocked him down again. After that he climbed a pipe onto the roof of a house and lay quiet until it began to get light. Since then he has been finding his way back. Then he asks if there is anything to drink.
hardWords: I thought it was time for me to be off

paragraphs.context: a huge animal bounded into view. As the moon was behind it
paragraphs.mainIdea: A huge animal jumps between Shasta and the desert and roars toward the desert. The cries of the other creatures stop, and then it turns to Shasta.
paragraphs.simple: Shasta was just going to run when a huge animal jumped into sight between him and the desert. The moon was behind it, so it looked quite black. Shasta did not know what it was. He saw only that it had a very big, shaggy head and four legs. It did not seem to see him. It suddenly stopped, turned its head toward the desert and roared. The roar rang through the Tombs and seemed to shake the sand under Shasta's feet. The cries of the other creatures suddenly stopped, and he thought he heard feet running away. Then the great beast turned to look at Shasta.

paragraphs.context: she never lost her head even for a moment
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aravis does not lose her head when the Narnians take Shasta away. Then a Tarkheena called Lasaraleen passes in a litter, and Aravis makes her first mistake.
paragraphs.simple: This is what had really happened. Aravis saw the Narnians hurry Shasta away, and she was left alone with two horses who very wisely said nothing. She never lost her head, even for a moment. She took Bree's halter and stood still, holding both horses. Her heart was beating as hard as a hammer, but she did nothing to show it. When the Narnian lords had passed, she tried to move on. But before she could take a step, another crier called out, "Way for the Tarkheena Lasaraleen!" Right after him came four armed slaves, and then four men carrying a litter. It had silk curtains that fluttered and silver bells that jingled, and it filled the whole street with the smell of perfume and flowers. After the litter came women slaves in beautiful clothes, and then a few grooms, runners, pages and others like them. And now Aravis made her first mistake.

paragraphs.context: First came the two slaves (deaf and dumb, as Aravis rightly guessed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aravis, hiding behind the sofa, sees who comes in: two slaves with candles, the very fat Tisroc, a tall young man and the new Grand Vizier. The Grand Vizier is the man she is to marry.
paragraphs.simple: First came two slaves, walking backward and carrying the candles. Aravis rightly guessed that they could not hear or speak, so they were used at the most secret meetings. One stood at each end of the sofa. That was good, because now it was harder to see Aravis. A slave was in front of her, and she looked out between his heels. Then came an old man, very fat, in a strange pointed cap. By the cap she knew he was the Tisroc. The smallest jewel he wore was worth more than all the clothes and weapons of the Narnian lords together. But he was so fat, and so covered with frills, pleats, buttons, tassels and charms, that Aravis thought the Narnian clothes (at least for men) looked nicer. After him came a tall young man in a turban with feathers and jewels, with a scimitar in an ivory case at his side. He seemed very excited, and his eyes and teeth flashed fiercely in the candlelight. Last came a little old man with a hump on his back. He had a wrinkled face. She knew with a shudder that he was Ahoshta Tarkaan, the new Grand Vizier and the man she was promised to marry.

paragraphs.context: This very night and in this hour I will take but two hundred horses
paragraphs.mainIdea: Rabadash tells his father his plan. He will ride to Anvard in two days and take it, go on to Cair Paravel, and catch Queen Susan when her ship arrives.
paragraphs.simple: Rabadash says that this very night he will take only two hundred horses and ride across the desert. It will seem to all men that his father knows nothing about it. On the second morning he will be at the gates of King Lune's castle of Anvard in Archenland. They are at peace with Calormen and not ready, and he will take Anvard before they can move. Then he will ride through the pass above Anvard and down through Narnia to Cair Paravel. The High King will not be there. He was getting ready for a raid against the giants on his northern border when Rabadash left. Rabadash will find Cair Paravel, most likely with open gates, and ride in. He will be careful and polite and spill as little Narnian blood as he can. Then he only has to sit there until the Splendor Hyaline comes in with Queen Susan on board. He will catch his lost bird as she steps ashore, swing her into the saddle and ride back to Anvard.

paragraphs.context: I also love none of these things in comparison with the glory and strength of my throne
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Tisroc says he loves the strength of his throne more than anything. If Rabadash wins, they get Archenland. If he fails, the Tisroc has eighteen other sons.
paragraphs.simple: The Tisroc says the Vizier's words are fine and right. He says he also loves none of these things as much as the glory and strength of his throne. If the Prince wins, they will have Archenland, and perhaps Narnia later. If he fails, the Tisroc has eighteen other sons. He says Rabadash, like the eldest sons of kings, was starting to be dangerous. More than five Tisrocs in Tashbaan died before their time, because their eldest sons grew tired of waiting for the throne. He says it is better for Rabadash to cool his blood far away than to boil it at home doing nothing. Then he says he wants to sleep. He tells the Vizier to send the musicians to his room. He also tells him to call back the pardon they wrote for the third cook, because he feels he will have a bad stomach.

paragraphs.context: one of the worst results of being a slave and being forced to do things
paragraphs.mainIdea: Hwin says nothing back to Bree, but she is right. The writer says a slave who is no longer forced almost loses the power to force himself.
paragraphs.simple: Hwin made no answer. Like most mares of good breeding, she was very nervous and gentle, and she was easily put down. But she was quite right. If Bree had had a Tarkaan on his back to make him go on, he would have found he could go for several hours of hard going. The writer says one of the worst results of being a slave is this. When no one forces you any more, you find that you have almost lost the power to force yourself.

paragraphs.context: One of the most terrible noises in the world, a horse's scream
paragraphs.mainIdea: A lion attacks Hwin and Aravis. Shasta has no weapon, but he shouts at the lion, and it suddenly turns and runs away.
paragraphs.simple: Hwin screamed, which is one of the most terrible sounds in the world. Aravis was bent low over Hwin's neck and seemed to be trying to draw her sword. Then Aravis, Hwin and the lion were almost on top of Shasta. Before they reached him, the lion rose on its back legs, larger than you would think a lion could be. It struck at Aravis with its right paw, and Shasta saw all the terrible claws stretched out. Aravis screamed and swayed in the saddle. The lion was tearing her shoulders. Shasta was half mad with horror. He had no weapon, not even a stick or a stone. He managed to stagger toward the lion and shouted at it, as one would at a dog, "Go home! Go home!" For a fraction of a second he was looking right into its wide-open mouth. Then, to his great surprise, the lion stopped itself, turned head over heels, got up and ran away.

paragraphs.context: I was the lion who forced you to join with Aravis
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Voice tells Shasta that it was the lion, and also the cat. It was also the one who pushed his boat to shore when he was a child.
paragraphs.simple: The Voice said it was the lion. Shasta stared with his mouth open and said nothing. The Voice said it was the lion who forced him to join with Aravis. It was the cat who comforted him among the houses of the dead. It was the lion who drove the jackals away while he slept. It was the lion who gave the Horses new strength, from fear, for the last mile, so that he would reach King Lune in time. And it was the lion he does not remember. That lion pushed the boat in which he lay as a child near death. The boat came to shore where a man sat awake at midnight to receive him.

paragraphs.context: Luckily Shasta had lived all his life too far south in Calormen
paragraphs.mainIdea: Shasta has not heard the true stories about Aslan. After one look at the Lion's face, he falls at its feet and says nothing.
paragraphs.simple: Shasta had lived all his life too far south in Calormen to have heard the tales whispered in Tashbaan. They were about a dreadful Narnian demon in the form of a lion. He knew none of the true stories about Aslan, the great Lion. Aslan is the son of the Emperor over-the-Sea and the King above all High Kings in Narnia. But after one look at the Lion's face, Shasta slipped out of the saddle and fell at its feet. He could not say anything, but he did not want to say anything, and he knew he did not need to.

paragraphs.context: It was all new and wonderful to Shasta for Calormene food is quite different
paragraphs.mainIdea: Everything in the Dwarfs' house is new to Shasta. After the meal the Dwarfs and Shasta sit outside in the sun.
paragraphs.simple: All this was new and wonderful to Shasta, because Calormene food is quite different. He did not know what the slices of brown stuff were, because he had never seen toast. He did not know the yellow soft thing was butter, because in Calormen you nearly always get oil. The house was also quite different from Arsheesh's dark hut that smelled of fish. It was different from the halls of the palaces in Tashbaan, which had pillars and carpets. The roof was very low, and everything was made of wood. There was a cuckoo-clock, a red-and-white checked tablecloth and a bowl of wild flowers. There were little curtains on the thick-paned windows. It was rather hard to use dwarf cups, plates, knives and forks. So the helpings were very small, but there were many, and Shasta's plate or cup was filled every moment. The Dwarfs kept asking for butter, more coffee, a few more mushrooms or another egg. When they had all eaten as much as they could, the three Dwarfs drew lots for who would do the washing-up, and Rogin was the unlucky one. Then Duffle and Bricklethumb took Shasta outside to a bench along the cottage wall. They stretched out their legs and gave a great sigh of contentment, and the two Dwarfs lit their pipes. The dew was off the grass and the sun was warm. It would have been too hot if there had not been a light breeze.

paragraphs.context: in a second he and the Dwarf were at it hammer and tongs
paragraphs.mainIdea: Corin and the Dwarf Thornbut begin to fight. It stops when Thornbut falls and sprains his ankle, which keeps him from walking or riding for at least a fortnight.
paragraphs.simple: That was enough for a boy like Corin, and in a second he and the Dwarf were fighting hard. It would have been an even match. Corin had longer arms and more height, but the Dwarf was older and tougher. But the fight was never finished, which is the worst of fights on a rough hillside. By very bad luck Thornbut stepped on a loose stone and fell flat on his nose. When he tried to get up, he found he had sprained his ankle. It was a very painful sprain, and it would keep him from walking or riding for at least a fortnight.

paragraphs.context: The unfortunate Rabadash appeared to be suspended from the castle walls
paragraphs.mainIdea: After the battle, everyone laughs at Rabadash, who hangs from a hook on the castle wall. A tear in the back of his chain mail caught on the hook when he jumped down.
paragraphs.simple: Shasta got up, feeling very stiff, and ran toward the sound to see what the joke was. He saw a very odd sight. Rabadash seemed to be hanging from the castle walls. His feet, about two feet from the ground, were kicking wildly. His chain-shirt was pulled up, so that it was tight under the arms and came halfway over his face. He looked like a man caught getting into a stiff shirt that is a little too small. People said later that this was what happened. Early in the battle, a Giant tried to stamp on Rabadash with his spiked boot. It did not crush him, as the Giant meant, but one of the spikes tore the chain mail. So when Rabadash met Edmund at the gate, he had a hole in the back of his hauberk. Edmund pressed him back toward the wall. Rabadash jumped up on a mounting block and hit down at Edmund from above. But there he was an easy mark for every arrow from the Narnian bows, so he decided to jump down. He wanted to look and sound very grand and dreadful as he jumped, crying, "The bolt of Tash falls from above." But he had to jump sideways, because the crowd left no room in front. Then the tear in his hauberk caught on a hook in the wall. Long ago the hook had had a ring for tying horses. So he hung there, like washing hung up to dry, with everyone laughing at him.

paragraphs.context: while Bree spoke they saw an enormous lion leap up from outside
paragraphs.mainIdea: While Bree talks, a huge lion jumps onto the wall and comes quietly toward him from behind. Hwin and Aravis see it and cannot make a sound.
paragraphs.simple: Bree stood with his back to the green wall while he spoke, and the other two faced him. He spoke in a rather superior tone with his eyes half shut. So he did not see the changed look on the faces of Hwin and Aravis. They had good reason to stare with open mouths. While Bree spoke, they saw an enormous lion leap up from outside and stand on top of the green wall. It was a brighter yellow, and bigger, and more beautiful and more alarming than any Lion they had seen. At once it jumped down inside the wall and began to come toward Bree from behind. It made no noise at all. Hwin and Aravis could not make any noise either, as if they were frozen.

paragraphs.context: The scratches on your back, tear for tear, throb for throb
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan tells Aravis why he scratched her. Her scratches were equal to the stripes laid on the back of her stepmother's slave. She needed to know what it felt like.
paragraphs.simple: Aslan says the scratches on Aravis's back were equal to the stripes laid on the back of her stepmother's slave. It was tear for tear, throb for throb and blood for blood. The slave was beaten because of the drugged sleep that Aravis put on her. Aslan says Aravis needed to know what it felt like.

paragraphs.context: A day will come when that boy will save Archenland from the deadliest danger
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cor tells how the Centaur said he would save Archenland. Lord Bar took Cor to sea, and King Lune went after him.
paragraphs.simple: Cor says that when the Centaur saw Corin and him, the Centaur looked at him. The Centaur said that a day would come when that boy would save Archenland from the deadliest danger it ever lay in. His father and mother were very pleased, but someone there was not. This was Lord Bar, who had been Lune's Lord Chancellor. Bar had done something wrong, and the King had had to dismiss him. Nothing else was done to him, and he could go on living in Archenland. But he had been in the pay of the Tisroc and had sent a lot of secret information to Tashbaan. When he heard that Cor would save Archenland from a great danger, he decided Cor must be put out of the way. He kidnapped Cor and rode down the Winding Arrow to the coast. A ship with his own followers was ready for him. He put out to sea with Cor on board. King Lune got wind of it, though not quite in time, and went after him as fast as he could. Lord Bar was already at sea when the King reached the coast, but not out of sight. Within twenty minutes the King was on board one of his own warships.

paragraphs.context: They couldn't help it. Rabadash had been wagging his ears all the time
paragraphs.mainIdea: At Aslan's words, Rabadash's ears, face and arms change until he is a donkey, and everyone laughs. His speech lasts a moment longer than his shape.
paragraphs.simple: They could not help laughing. Rabadash had been wagging his ears all the time, and as soon as Aslan said, "The hour has struck!" the ears began to change. They grew longer and more pointed, and soon had gray hair on them. Everyone was wondering where they had seen ears like that, when Rabadash's face began to change too. It grew longer, and thicker at the top, and the eyes grew larger. The nose sank back into the face, or else the face swelled out and became all nose, and there was hair all over it. His arms grew longer and came down in front of him until his hands rested on the ground. They were not hands now, they were hoofs. He was standing on all fours, and his clothes disappeared. Everyone laughed louder and louder, because now what had been Rabadash was a donkey. The terrible thing was that his human speech lasted just a moment longer than his human shape. So when he saw the change coming over him, he screamed.

paragraphs.context: And in the temple of Tash you shall be healed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan says Rabadash will be healed in the temple of Tash at the Autumn Feast. If he ever goes more than ten miles from the great temple in Tashbaan, he will become a donkey again for good.
paragraphs.simple: Aslan tells Rabadash that he has appealed to Tash, so in the temple of Tash he will be healed. He must stand before the altar of Tash in Tashbaan at the great Autumn Feast this year. There, in the sight of all Tashbaan, his ass's shape will fall from him, and all men will know him for Prince Rabadash. But as long as he lives, if he ever goes more than ten miles away from the great temple in Tashbaan, he will at once be as he is now. And from that second change there will be no return.

paragraphs.context: For this is what it means to be a king: to be first in every desperate attack
paragraphs.mainIdea: King Lune tells Cor what it means to be a king. A king is first in attack and last in retreat. When there is hunger, he wears finer clothes and laughs louder over a smaller meal.
paragraphs.simple: King Lune says that this is truer than Cor's brother knows. He says being a king means to be first in every desperate attack and last in every desperate retreat. It also means that when there is hunger in the land, which must be now and then in bad years, the king wears finer clothes. He also laughs louder over a smaller meal than any man in the land.

sentences.context: Shasta, who had never learned that it is wrong to listen behind doors
sentences.simple: Shasta had never learned that it is wrong to listen behind doors. So he sat with his ear to a crack in the wall of the cottage to hear what the grown-ups said.
sentences.grammar: 'who had never learned' is a relative clause giving extra news about Shasta; 'had learned' (past perfect) looks back to a time before he sat down.

sentences.context: you'd better be lying dead tonight than go to be a human slave
sentences.simple: It would be better for you to be dead tonight than to go to his house tomorrow as a human slave.
sentences.grammar: 'had better X than Y' says X is the better choice than Y, so Y must be very bad.

sentences.context: as you and I would feel if we had just overheard our parents
sentences.simple: Do not think that Shasta felt as you and I would feel if we had just heard our parents talk about selling us for slaves.
sentences.grammar: 'would feel if we had just overheard' pictures an imagined case that is not real; 'must not imagine' tells the reader not to think so.

sentences.context: It would be dreadful to find, when I get back to Narnia
sentences.simple: It would be terrible to find, when I get back to Narnia, that I have picked up a lot of low, bad habits.
sentences.grammar: 'would be dreadful' is a worry about something that might be true; 'I've picked up' (present perfect) means he already has the habits, and 'pick up' means learn.

sentences.context: well, if that's not fishy, call me a cob
sentences.simple: A high-born Tarkheena rides alone at night in her brother's armor and wants no questions. If that is not strange, then call me a cob!
sentences.grammar: 'if that's not fishy, call me a cob' means 'I am sure it is fishy (strange and not honest)'; 'call me X' is a way to say 'I will be X if I am wrong'.

sentences.context: Everyone had been putting off this difficulty
sentences.simple: Everyone had been putting off this problem. But now they could not put it off any longer.
sentences.grammar: 'had been putting off' (past perfect continuous) shows they had done it for some time before; 'could be put off no longer' is a passive: nobody could wait any more.

sentences.context: one usually gets on better with people when one is making plans
sentences.simple: Aravis became a little less unfriendly to Shasta during these talks. People get on better when they make plans than when they talk about nothing in particular.
sentences.grammar: 'One' means 'a person in general' (formal); 'gets on better ... when ... than when ...' compares two times, and 'get on' means be friendly.

sentences.context: you would be happy, for in that land no maiden is forced to marry against her will
sentences.simple: If you were in Narnia you would be happy, because in that land no girl is forced to marry against her will.
sentences.grammar: 'If you were ... you would be' is an imagined case; 'is forced to marry' is a passive (someone makes her), and 'against her will' means she does not want it.

sentences.context: it would have been better if he had held his tongue
sentences.simple: It would have been better if Shasta had kept quiet. The soldier hit him on the side of the face and nearly knocked him down.
sentences.grammar: 'would have been better if he had held' is an unreal past case: he did not keep quiet; 'hold one's tongue' means stay silent.

sentences.context: everyone who is less important has to get out of the way for everyone who is more important
sentences.simple: In Tashbaan there is one rule for the traffic. Everyone who is less important has to get out of the way for everyone who is more important. If not, you get a cut from a whip or a punch from the end of a spear.
sentences.grammar: 'which is that ...' explains what the rule is; 'has to' means must; 'unless' means 'if not'.

sentences.context: could find it in your heart to show him so much favor
sentences.simple: I was surprised that you could ever be willing to show him so much favor.
sentences.grammar: 'it was a wonder to me that ...' is old, formal English for 'I was surprised that ...'; 'find it in your heart to' means be willing to.

sentences.context: Easily in but not easily out, as the lobster said in the lobster pot
sentences.simple: It is easy to get in but not easy to get out, as the lobster said in the lobster pot!
sentences.grammar: A short saying with the verb left out: 'easily in but not easily out' means easy to get in but not easy to get out; 'as ... said' gives the lobster's words as a joke.

sentences.context: Oh, if only I had never left Cair Paravel
sentences.simple: I wish I had never left Cair Paravel.
sentences.grammar: 'if only + had + past participle' is a wish about the past: she did leave, and it cannot be changed.

sentences.context: how would it be if your Majesties bade the Prince to a great banquet
sentences.simple: What if you asked the Prince to a great feast on board our own ship, the Splendor Hyaline, tomorrow night?
sentences.grammar: 'how would it be if ...?' is an old way to suggest an idea ('what if ...?'); 'bade' is the past of 'bid', here meaning 'asked'.

sentences.context: If they knew I wasn't one of themselves, they'd never let me out of this house alive
sentences.simple: If they knew I was not one of them, they would never let me leave this house alive.
sentences.grammar: 'If + past (knew), would + verb' pictures an imagined case: they do not know now, but this is what would follow if they did.

sentences.context: there is a great difference between a noise heard letting you in with your friends
sentences.simple: A noise in the morning that lets you in with your friends is very different from a noise at nightfall that shuts you out when you are alone.
sentences.grammar: 'a noise heard ...' uses a past participle to mean 'a noise that is heard'; 'letting you in' and 'shutting you out' say what each noise does.

sentences.context: if he had read as many books as you have about journeys over deserts
sentences.simple: It was a crazy idea. If Shasta had read as many books as you have about journeys over deserts, he would never have thought of it.
sentences.grammar: 'If he had read ..., he would never have dreamed' is an unreal past case: he had read no books, so he did dream of it.

sentences.context: If you had given me the swiftest of the galleys at sunrise
sentences.simple: If you had given me the fastest ship at sunrise, when I first saw the ship of the barbarians was gone, I might have caught them.
sentences.grammar: 'If you had given ..., I would perhaps have overtaken' is an unreal past case: the Tisroc did not give the ship, so Rabadash did not catch them.

sentences.context: I am determined not to put my hand out farther than I can draw it back
sentences.simple: I have firmly decided not to put my hand out farther than I can pull it back.
sentences.grammar: 'determined not to + verb' means firmly decided not to; 'farther than I can draw it back' is a picture: do not reach out more than you can pull back.

sentences.context: He had better cool his blood abroad than boil it in inaction here
sentences.simple: It is better for him to cool his blood in another country than to boil it here doing nothing.
sentences.grammar: 'had better X than Y' means X is the wiser choice than Y; 'cool his blood' and 'boil it' are pictures for becoming calm and for staying angry.

sentences.context: Shasta would nearly have fallen asleep if he had not had to dismount
sentences.simple: Shasta would almost have fallen asleep if he had not had to get off and walk now and then.
sentences.grammar: 'would nearly have fallen asleep if he had not had to' is an unreal past case: he had to walk, so he did not fall asleep.

sentences.context: He had not yet learned that if you do one good deed
sentences.simple: Shasta did not yet know this: when you do one good thing, you are usually given another, harder and better thing to do.
sentences.grammar: 'had not yet learned' (past perfect) means he did not know it before then; 'is to be set to do' is a passive meaning 'is given a job to do'.

sentences.context: have yet little knowledge of things future
sentences.simple: I know many things that are happening now by my art, but I still know little about things in the future.
sentences.grammar: 'things future' puts the adjective after the noun (old style, 'future things'); 'yet' here means 'still'.

sentences.context: If the horse had been any good—or if he had known how to get any good out of the horse
sentences.simple: If the horse had been any good, or if Shasta had known how to get any use out of it, he would have risked a wild gallop. But he knew he could not make that horse gallop.
sentences.grammar: 'If ... had been ..., he would have risked' is an unreal past case; 'any good' means at all good, and 'get good out of' means get some use from.

sentences.context: somebody ought to tell someone about it with a view to doing something
sentences.simple: The Rabbit agreed that this was very surprising news. He said somebody ought to tell someone, so that something could be done.
sentences.grammar: 'with a view to + -ing' means 'with the aim of doing'; 'ought to' means should.

sentences.context: But if you would not be taken for one, another time try not to hear what's meant for other ears
sentences.simple: If you do not want people to think you are a traitor, next time try not to hear what was not meant for you.
sentences.grammar: 'taken for' means thought to be; 'if you would not be ...' means 'if you do not want to be ...'; 'what's meant for other ears' means words said for other people.

sentences.context: He would have been wiser if he had set his men to making ladders
sentences.simple: He would have been wiser if he had told his men to make ladders. But that takes too long, and he cannot wait.
sentences.grammar: 'would have been wiser if he had set' is an unreal past case; 'set his men to making' means gave his men the job of making.

sentences.context: He ought to have ridden back to Tashbaan as soon as the first attack failed
sentences.simple: He should have ridden back to Tashbaan as soon as the first attack failed, because his whole plan needed speed and surprise.
sentences.grammar: 'ought to have + past participle' says what was right to do in the past but was not done.

sentences.context: His Highness would not be your son if he did not inherit your conditions
sentences.simple: His Highness would not be your son if he did not have your nature.
sentences.grammar: 'would not be ... if he did not' is an imagined case; 'conditions' is an old word here meaning a person's nature.

sentences.context: I'd be just as pleased—or very nearly—at finding he's my father even if he weren't a king
sentences.simple: I would be almost as happy to find he is my father even if he were not a king.
sentences.grammar: 'even if he weren't' uses 'were' for an imagined case; 'pleased at finding' is a preposition followed by -ing.

sentences.context: Do not dare not to dare
sentences.simple: Do not be afraid to be bold.
sentences.grammar: 'Do not dare not to dare' is a word play: 'dare' means have the courage, so it means 'do not be afraid to be bold'.

sentences.context: Hast no more power to start away from thy crown than any sentry from his post
sentences.simple: You have no more power to leave your crown than a guard has to leave his place.
sentences.grammar: Old English: 'hast' is 'have' and 'thy' is 'your'; 'no more ... than' means 'just as little as'.

sentences.context: what Rabadash hadn't realized is that it is very easy to frighten people who know
sentences.simple: Rabadash had not seen that it is easy to frighten people who know you can have them boiled alive as soon as you say so.
sentences.grammar: 'what Rabadash hadn't realized' is a noun clause that is the subject; 'hadn't realized' (past perfect) looks back from the time of the scene.

find fault with.meaning: To keep saying what is wrong with someone or something.
find fault with.example: he would find fault with him and perhaps beat him

turn out.meaning: To make someone leave a place.
turn out.example: was given a hunk of bread and turned out of the cottage

run away.meaning: To leave a place and try not to be found.

hold on.meaning: To keep your hold on something so that you do not fall.
hold on.example: If I'm not to hold on by the reins

pick up.meaning: To learn or get something, such as a habit, without trying.
pick up.example: that I've picked up a lot of low, bad habits

put off.meaning: To leave something until a later time.
put off.example: Everyone had been putting off this difficulty

get through.meaning: To pass through a place without being stopped.
get through.example: how they were to get through it

go on.meaning: To keep doing something, or to keep talking.
go on.example: It went on tearing up the grass

get on with.meaning: To keep doing something you were doing.
get on with.example: But get on with the story

fall in with.example: I fell in with her in the forest

hold one's tongue.meaning: To say nothing and keep silent.
hold one's tongue.example: it would have been better if he had held his tongue

make oneself scarce.meaning: To go away so that nobody sees you.
make oneself scarce.example: tried to make himself scarce in the crowd

turn up.meaning: To arrive or appear, often when it is not expected.
turn up.example: would not turn up until it was too late

give up.meaning: To stop trying to do something.
give up.example: he soon gave up trying to count them

catch sight of.meaning: To see something for a short moment.
catch sight of.example: Shasta caught sight of green branches

make much of.meaning: To show a lot of care and attention to someone.
make much of.example: he was made much of and laid on a sofa

prick up one's ears.meaning: To start to listen with great interest.
prick up one's ears.example: Shasta pricked up his ears at this point

knock down.meaning: To hit someone so that they fall to the ground.
knock down.example: So I fought the Watch and they knocked me down

give away.meaning: To let people know a secret.
give away.example: she's given the whole thing away

set out.example: set out for Mount Pire alone

lose one's head.meaning: To become too afraid or excited to think clearly.
lose one's head.example: she never lost her head even for a moment

doze off.meaning: To go to sleep, often for a short time.

make the best of.meaning: To do as well as you can when things are not good.
make the best of.example: but she had to make the best of it

give in.meaning: To stop saying no and do what someone else wants.
give in.example: she had to give in to Aravis

come to oneself.meaning: To wake up after you were hurt or fainted.
come to oneself.example: When Aravis came to herself she found that she was lying

make a face.meaning: To twist your face to show you do not like something.
make a face.example: Aravis couldn't help making a face when she tasted it

take stock of.meaning: To look carefully at what is around you.
take stock of.example: began to take stock of his surroundings

see to.meaning: To make sure that something happens.
see to.example: I would see to it that he died

look in on.meaning: To visit someone for a short time.
look in on.example: Naturally we'd look in on him and say good-bye

draw near.example: you poor, proud frightened Horse, draw near

get wind of.meaning: To hear about something that is secret.
get wind of.example: But Father got wind of it

put out to sea.meaning: To leave land in a ship.
put out to sea.example: he put out to sea with me on board

keep up with.meaning: To go as fast as someone or something.
keep up with.example: keeping up with the galloping horses
